proposed.explanation:
You already hold 300 shares of COMI (Commercial International Bank of Egypt), which aligns directly with your stated goal of growing savings steadily with a bank stock over a 5-year horizon. The FY2025 results show strong and accelerating fundamentals: net profit rose roughly 49% year-on-year (from 55.26 billion EGP to 82.26 billion EGP), net interest income grew about 18% (from 91.06 billion to 107.70 billion EGP), and total assets expanded about 19% (from 1,215.0 billion to 1,442.5 billion EGP). Basic EPS increased from 14.72 to 18.25 EGP per share. At the current price of 128 EGP, the implied P/E is approximately 7.0×, which is reasonable for a bank delivering this growth rate and does not suggest the stock is overvalued.

I am recommending you hold rather than buy more because your COMI position already represents about 56% of your total portfolio (38,400 EGP in shares out of 68,400 EGP total). The diversification rule caps any single holding at 50% of portfolio value after a buy, and since you are already above that threshold, purchasing additional shares is not permitted. Selling would also be counterproductive given your explicit goal of growing with a bank stock and your 5-year horizon; the medium risk profile is consistent with holding a large, profitable bank.

Risks and uncertainties: the evidence covers only two fiscal years of income-statement and balance-sheet data. I do not have information on loan-loss provisions, capital adequacy ratios, non-performing loan trends, dividend policy, or the competitive/regulatory environment. A P/E of ~7× could reflect market concerns not visible in these figures. The 49% profit jump, while impressive, may not be sustainable every year. Your portfolio is concentrated in a single stock, which amplifies idiosyncratic risk. I recommend monitoring COMI's quarterly results and considering adding a second, uncorrelated holding in the future to bring the bank position below 50% of the portfolio. This is guidance, not a guarantee of returns.

limitations: Only two fiscal years of income-statement and balance-sheet data are available; no quarterly trend, no cash-flow statement, no dividend history.
No information on loan-loss provisions, non-performing loan ratios, capital adequacy, or regulatory constraints.

The EPS figures carry a page-level unit of 'EGP thousands,' which is atypical for a per-share metric; I have interpreted them as EGP per share, which is the standard convention. If the unit were applied literally, the P/E calculation would change.
No peer comparison or sector context is provided, so the ~7× P/E cannot be benchmarked against other Egyptian banks.
The 49% profit growth may include one-off items not visible in the condensed statements.
